Fatfleshed
făt´flĕsht
adj. (well-fed; fat in body)
A compound of fat + fleshed, formed to render the Hebrew phrase exactly. It occurs twice, both in Pharaoh's dream of the seven kine, and in both places it is paired with well favoured.

Biblical Definition

The dream that moved Joseph from a prison to a throne opens with cattle: “And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed; and they fed in a meadow” (Genesis 41:2). Pharaoh recounts it himself in the same words: “And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow” (Genesis 41:18). What follows is the detail no one in Egypt could explain: “And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke” (Genesis 41:4). The lean did not merely replace the fat; they consumed them and were no better for it, which is exactly how a seven-year famine consumes a seven-year surplus. Joseph refuses credit for the interpretation and gives the reason the dream came twice: “And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass” (Genesis 41:32). The fatfleshed kine are plenty, and plenty in Scripture is never self-explaining. It is a season God grants, with a term, and the wise man is the one who is told how long it lasts and believes it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fat as fleshy; plump; of full or plump habit of body, and kine as the plural of cow.

expand to see more

FAT, a. Fleshy; plump; round; of full or plump habit of body; abounding with fat.

FLESHED, a. Fed with flesh; having flesh; used in composition, as fat-fleshed, lean-fleshed.

KINE, n. plu. of cow; cows; the old plural form retained in Scripture.

MEADOW, n. A tract of low land, appropriated to the culture of grass for hay.

FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.

Key Scripture

Genesis 41:2 — "And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed ; and they fed in a meadow."

Genesis 41:18 — "And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow:"

Genesis 41:4 — "And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke."

Genesis 41:32 — "And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass."

Modern Corruption

The account is treated as a folk tale about a clever dream-reader, which removes the claim the chapter actually makes — that God established the thing and sent the warning.

expand to see more

Read as ancient literature, Genesis 41 is a court tale of the wise courtier who rises by his wits, a type found across the Near East. The chapter anticipates exactly that reading and refuses it in Joseph's first sentence to Pharaoh: it is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. Joseph claims no skill, gives no technique, and attributes both dream and interpretation to God. The doubling of the dream is likewise explained not as literary emphasis but as divine confirmation — the thing is established by God. To read the chapter as a tale of shrewdness is to delete the only explanation the text offers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the doctrine of seasons of plenty. Seven fat years were a gift and they were also a deadline, and the fat kine were eaten by the lean ones. Scripture's consistent counsel about abundance is that it is temporary, that it is given to be administered rather than consumed, and that the man who reads plenty as permanence is the fool of the parable whose barns were full the night his soul was required of him. Joseph's storehouses were an act of faith in a word from God about a famine no one could yet see.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew beri basar, fat of flesh; parah (H6510), a cow or heifer; ra ab (H7458), famine; chalom (H2472), a dream.

expand to see more

Hebrew bari (H1277) — fat, fatfleshed; the well favoured kine of Genesis 41:2.

Hebrew basar (H1320) — flesh; the second half of the compound.

Hebrew parah (H6510) — a cow, heifer; the kine coming up out of the river.

Hebrew chalom (H2472) — a dream; doubled to Pharaoh as confirmation.

Hebrew raab (H7458) — famine, hunger; the seven years the lean kine signified.

Usage

"“Seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed” — the years of plenty."

"“The ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine” — famine consuming surplus."

"“The thing is established by God” — why the dream came twice."
